blocks.text: 1. Keyword Search

blocks.alt: Query terms go through exact term match to produce results

blocks.text: Semantic Search covered meaning based matching. Keyword Search addresses exactly the gap semantic search left open, matching exact terms instead of underlying meaning.
It matches literal words and phrases rather than underlying meaning.
2. The Weakness This Method Fixes
A specific code, error message, or proper noun can get lost among semantically similar but wrong matches.
Keyword search was built specifically to guarantee exact term matches.
3. How Keyword Search Actually Works
As with one position per term in Sparse Embeddings, keyword search checks whether specific terms literally appear in a chunk.
No meaning or context gets considered, only the presence of the terms themselves.
4. Scoring Relevance With TF-IDF

blocks.alt: Term frequency and inverse document frequency combine into a score

blocks.text: As with the classical roots of TF-IDF in Sparse Embeddings, rare terms get weighted higher than common ones.
A chunk matching several rare, distinctive terms scores higher than one matching common words.

blocks.text: 5. BM25 As The Modern Standard

blocks.alt: TF-IDF is compared against BM25, the modern standard

blocks.text: BM25 refines TF-IDF by capping how much repeated term frequency can inflate a score.
It's widely used as the default keyword scoring algorithm in modern search systems today.
6. Exact Match Precision

blocks.alt: An exact term like invoice number 4521 gives a precise match

blocks.text: A specific product code or error message matches precisely, with zero ambiguity.
As with exact match strength in Sparse Embeddings, no paraphrase confusion ever enters into it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Searching for the exact error code "ERR_504" finds only chunks containing that precise string under keyword search, with none of the paraphrase drift a semantic search over similar sounding text could introduce.

blocks.text: 7. Weakness: Keyword Search Cannot Paraphrase

blocks.alt: The keyword car misses the paraphrase automobile

blocks.text: As with meaning over keywords in Semantic Search, a query worded differently from the source text can miss a relevant chunk entirely.
Keyword search alone is not always enough on its own, either.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A user asking "how do I sign in again" when the source document says "authenticate your account" would not match under keyword search alone, since neither phrasing shares exact terms with the other.

blocks.text: 8. Indexing For Keyword Search

blocks.alt: Documents build an inverted index for fast term lookup

blocks.text: As with what an index actually does in Indexing, a keyword index maps each term to the list of chunks containing it.
This enables fast lookup without scanning every chunk's full text on every query.
9. Recognizing When Keyword Search Is The Right Retrieval Method

blocks.alt: Needing exact term or code matching points toward keyword search

blocks.text: Precise codes, error messages, and proper nouns suit keyword search well.
Conceptual, natural language questions favor semantic search instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates a simplified TF-IDF style keyword search over a small chunk collection.

code.content:
import math

chunks = [
    {"id": "c1", "text": "The refund policy allows returns within thirty days."},
    {"id": "c2", "text": "Shipping timelines vary by region and product type."},
    {"id": "c3", "text": "Refund requests for damaged products are processed quickly."},
]

def term_frequency(term, text):
    words = text.lower().split()
    return words.count(term.lower()) / len(words)

def inverse_document_frequency(term, chunks):
    # scoring relevance with TF-IDF
    containing = sum(1 for c in chunks if term.lower() in c["text"].lower())
    return math.log(len(chunks) / (1 + containing)) + 1

def tfidf_score(query, chunk, chunks):
    terms = query.lower().split()
    score = 0
    for term in terms:
        tf = term_frequency(term, chunk["text"])
        idf = inverse_document_frequency(term, chunks)
        score += tf * idf
    return score

query = "refund"
print(f"Query (how keyword search actually works): {query!r}\n")
results = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: -tfidf_score(query, c, chunks))
for c in results:
    score = tfidf_score(query, c, chunks)
    print(f" {c['id']}: {score:.3f} - {c['text']}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the two chunks containing the exact word "refund" scoring highest, while the unrelated shipping chunk scores zero.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using keyword search alone for conceptual queries that need paraphrase matching.
Ignoring term rarity weighting, treating common and distinctive words as equally important.
Assuming keyword search understands synonyms or related phrasing the way semantic search does.
Skipping a proper keyword index and scanning full chunk text on every single query.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Keyword search matches literal words and phrases rather than underlying meaning.
It was built specifically to guarantee exact matches that semantic search alone can miss.
It checks whether specific terms literally appear in a chunk, with no meaning considered.
Rare, distinctive terms get weighted higher than common words under TF-IDF style scoring.
BM25 refines TF-IDF and is widely used as the default keyword scoring algorithm today.
Exact codes and error messages match with zero ambiguity, unlike semantic search.
Keyword search cannot handle paraphrased or differently worded queries.
A keyword index maps each term to the chunks containing it for fast lookup.
